+

HFT Practice · Lesson 0035

+

Feature Contracts at Inference: Train/Serve Skew and the Last-Bar Problem

+
Why this matters here: your model bundles are saved as +{"model": ..., "features": [...]} and CLAUDE.md warns that the +features list "defines exact column order at inference." This lesson explains +what that contract really is, how build_features silently eats the one row you +most want to predict on, and why strategies/gbm_adapter.py pads the frame with a +copy of the last bar.
+ +

1 · The concept: a feature contract

+

When you train a model on a table of features, you implicitly sign a contract with your +future self. At inference time you must reproduce:

+ + + + + + +
ClauseMeaningWhat breaks if violated
NamesThe same columns existKeyError, or silently missing features filled with garbage
OrderColumns feed the model in training orderNo error at all — sklearn sees a bare numpy array and happily multiplies RSI by the coefficient it learned for volume. Predictions are nonsense.
SemanticsEach column is computed the same waySubtle drift: RSI via rolling mean ≠ RSI via EMA (Wilder). Same name, different number.
AvailabilityEvery input is knowable at decision timeLookahead bias (using tomorrow) or inference lag (using yesterday when today exists)
+

Violating any clause produces train/serve skew: the model runs on inputs +distributionally different from what it was trained on. The insidious part is that clauses +2–4 usually fail silently — the code runs, numbers come out, and the equity curve +quietly rots.

+ +

2 · Minimal standalone example

+
# The last-bar problem in eight lines.
+import pandas as pd
+
+close = pd.Series([100, 102, 101, 105], name="close")
+df = pd.DataFrame({"close": close})
+df["ret_1d"]     = df["close"].pct_change()   # backward-looking: fine today
+df["fwd_ret_1d"] = df["ret_1d"].shift(-1)      # the TARGET: tomorrow's return
+
+# Row 3 (today, close=105) has fwd_ret_1d = NaN — tomorrow hasn't happened.
+# That is CORRECT for training: you can't learn from an unknown label.
+clean = df.dropna()   # ...but dropna() just deleted TODAY —
+                      # the only row you actually want to predict on.
+

The target column must be NaN on the newest bar (anything else is lookahead). +A blanket dropna() is right for building a training set and wrong for building +an inference row. One function serving both callers is where the bug lives.

+ +

3 · In this project

+ +

paper_trading_sim.py:48–69 — the contract's single source of truth +build_features() produces close, ret_1d, ma_5, ma_10, ma_gap, vol_10, +rsi_14 plus the target fwd_ret_1d = ret_1d.shift(-1), then ends with +return out.dropna(). Every feature is backward-looking; only the target looks +forward. So on any frame, the final returned row is at best yesterday.

+ +

predict_next.py:136–144 — a live one-day inference lag (pre-existing quirk)

+
feats = build_features(df).dropna()
+# ...
+latest = feats.iloc[-1]   # ← looks like "today", is actually YESTERDAY:
+                          #   build_features' dropna removed today's row
+                          #   because today's TARGET is NaN.
+

The production predictor therefore forecasts tomorrow using features as of the most +recent complete bar — a full day stale. Availability clause violated in the +conservative direction: no cheating, but the model trades on old information. +(Found during the 2026-07-05 overnight session; deliberately not changed there because it +alters live behaviour — it deserves its own reviewed fix.)

+ +

strategies/gbm_adapter.py — the padding fix used by the Strategy Arena

+
padded = pd.concat([df, df.iloc[[-1]]])   # duplicate the newest bar
+feats = build_features(padded)
+

After padding, the real newest bar is no longer last, so its target becomes a +finite dummy (return vs. its own copy = 0) and it survives the dropna. The copy, now the +final row, inherits the NaN target and is dropped instead. Because every feature only +looks backward, the copy cannot contaminate the real bar's inputs. Result: true +same-day features from the unmodified production pipeline — the semantics clause +holds because there is still exactly one implementation of the features.

+ +

strategies/gbm_adapter.py — honouring the order clause

+
X = row[self._feat_cols].astype(float).values.reshape(1, -1)
+yhat = float(self._model.predict(X)[0])
+

self._feat_cols comes from the bundle's features list — never +from "whatever columns the frame has." Reindexing by the saved list is what enforces +name + order every single time.

+ +

4 · Often confused with

+ + + + + + +
Lookahead biasInference lag
What leaksFuture information leaks into features/decisionsNothing leaks — features are merely stale
Effect on backtestBacktest looks better than reality (the killer)Backtest and live both look slightly worse than necessary
Direction of errorOptimistic — you will lose real money finding outPessimistic/conservative — you leave edge on the table
In this repoGuarded by shift(-1) targets and walk-forward retraining cutoffs (f.index < dt)predict_next.py predicting off yesterday's row
+

Both are violations of the same availability clause — in opposite directions. +Lesson 0032 covered lookahead in candlestick detection; this is its mirror image. +Separately, don't confuse train/serve skew (inputs differ between training +and inference) with overfitting (model memorises noise in training data). +A perfectly regularised model still fails under skew, and the arena's +backtest-vs-live divergence column is designed to surface exactly that.

+ +

5 · Practice

+

Click an answer. Options are shuffled on every load. Score: 0 / 0

+ +
+

Q1. A saved bundle has features = ["close","ret_1d","rsi_14"]. + At inference you build a frame whose columns happen to be + ["rsi_14","close","ret_1d"] and call + model.predict(frame.values). What happens?

+
    +
  • sklearn raises a feature-name mismatch error
    • +
  • It runs without error and returns garbage predictions
    • +
  • pandas silently reorders the columns to match training
    • +
  • The predictions come back as NaN
    • +
+

+
+ +
+

Q2. Why is fwd_ret_1d NaN on the newest bar of every frame + build_features sees?

+
    +
  • Because yfinance hasn't finished downloading the latest row
    • +
  • Because RSI needs 14 bars of warmup
    • +
  • Because the target is tomorrow's return, and tomorrow hasn't happened
    • +
  • Because rolling windows make the newest row incomplete
    • +
+

+
+ +
+

Q3. In gbm_adapter.py, why can't the duplicated last bar + contaminate the real last bar's features?

+
    +
  • Because the copy is removed before features are computed
    • +
  • Because every feature only looks backward, and the copy sits after the real bar
    • +
  • Because pandas deduplicates repeated index dates automatically
    • +
  • Because the copy's target is NaN, so its features are ignored
    • +
+

+
+ +
+

Q4. Your arena report shows a strategy whose live Sharpe collapses far + below its backtest Sharpe. Feature code is identical in both paths. Which contract clause + is the FIRST suspect?

+
    +
  • Semantics — the indicator formulas drifted
    • +
  • Availability — live decisions use rows from a different time than backtest decisions
    • +
  • Names — a feature column went missing in live
    • +
  • Order — columns swapped between the two paths
    • +
+

+
+ +
+

Q5. Lookahead bias vs. inference lag — which statement is true?

+
    +
  • Inference lag inflates backtest results; lookahead deflates them
    • +
  • predict_next.py's iloc[-1] quirk is a lookahead bias
    • +
  • Lookahead makes results look too good; lag merely makes them stale and conservative
    • +
  • They are unrelated problems from different contract clauses
    • +
+

+
+ +

6 · Check your understanding (scenarios)

+
Scenario A. You add a news_sent_3d feature and retrain. Six months later a teammate "optimises" news_features.py to use a 5-day window but keeps the column name. What breaks, and would any test catch it? +

The semantics clause breaks: same name, different number, so the saved bundle +silently runs on a distribution it never trained on. Nothing crashes. A characterisation +test pinning known input → known feature values (like the golden values in +test_paper_trading.py) is the only automatic catch; otherwise it surfaces as unexplained +live-vs-backtest divergence in the arena report.

+
Scenario B. To "fix" the last-bar problem someone changes build_features to fillna(0) the target instead of dropping. Why is that worse than the padding trick? +

Every training set now contains a final row whose label claims "tomorrow's return was +exactly 0%" — a fabricated label fed into every retrain (including walkforward_sim's +rolling retrains, which call the same function). The padding trick keeps the fabricated +value outside the training path because it only exists in the inference call's +frame, and even there it's never used as an input.

+
Scenario C. The FPGA/C++ ONNX path (gradient_boosting/) re-implements feature computation in C++. Which clauses are at risk and what's the cheapest guard? +

Semantics (two implementations of RSI/MA can drift) and order (the ONNX input tensor is +positional). Cheapest guard: a golden-file test — one fixed OHLCV frame, feature vectors +computed by both Python and C++, asserted equal to tolerance. CLAUDE.md's rule "re-export +ONNX after changing build_features" exists exactly because of this risk.

+ +
+ + + + + + + +
+ + +
+ + Investigate per the method in your instructions, then return the findings list.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud (requires claude.ai account access)). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
